definitions.meaning: harness-racing horses that move at a two-beat gait
the feet on which pigs walk, sold by butchers as a cheap cut

explanation.surface: Some horses are made to carry pigs on their backs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carrying' looks like a link between the two nouns, but 'carrying pigs' is the second definition: the parts that carry a pig about are its feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share one word: racehorses bred for that gait, and pigs' feet as a butcher names them.

parts.note: keyed means tapped on keys, and the writer is a typing machine: tapping the keys of that machine

explanation.surface: An author who is tense and nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keyed up' looks like 'nervous'; it means struck on the keys, which is what this word means before 'writer'.
explanation.definitionFit: To press the keys of a writing machine is the verb; with writer it names the machine.

clue.text: Whom the poet wished we could view objectively

definitions.text: Whom the poet wished we could view objectively

parts.words: Whom the poet wished we could view objectively
parts.note: Robert Burns wrote 'O wad some Pow'r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us'

explanation.surface: A literary question about a poet's wish for clear sight.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet is Robert Burns, in 'To a Louse': he wished we could see us as others see us.
explanation.definitionFit: Burns asked to see us as others see us, that is, our own selves.

clue.text: Hawker's ballad bishop, suitably sleevy at last

definitions.text: Hawker's ballad bishop, suitably sleevy at last

parts.words: Hawker's ballad bishop, suitably sleevy at last
parts.note: Lawn sleeves are a bishop's dress, and the name holds LAWN with Y, the last of sleevy, at its end

explanation.surface: A bishop from a Cornish song, aptly ending in sleeves.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Stephen Hawker wrote the Cornish 'Song of the Western Men' about the bishop jailed in 1688; lawn sleeves are a bishop's robe, fittingly inside the name, which ends in Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Hawker's song honours the Cornish bishop Sir Jonathan, one of the Seven Bishops jailed by James II.

definitions.meaning: a castle piece standing on a chessboard square

explanation.surface: Dishonesty from someone who claims to be honest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the square' means honest; here it means sitting on a chessboard square, as the castle does.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to swindle, and the noun is the chess castle on its square.

parts.note: a revolt is an ..., and the young people of an era make up one age group, so a rebel band of youngsters is described

explanation.surface: A complaint about unruly teenagers.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase normally means the young people coming up behind their elders; the clue reads its first word as 'in revolt'.
explanation.definitionFit: The stock phrase names young people growing up, and the first word can also mean an insurrection.

indicators.note: the letters of no vile are arranged in an entirely different way

explanation.surface: A state that is not vile at all, rather the opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quite otherwise' rearranges NO VILE; the surface also hints that being smitten is the opposite of vile.
explanation.definitionFit: Being smitten with someone is a state or condition one is in.

parts.note: to hint is to leave a thing unsaid that listeners still grasp

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise followed by sympathy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You don't say!' looks like surprise; read literally, you don't state it, yet we understand it: a hint.
explanation.definitionFit: To suggest without stating is to convey meaning that is not said outright.

clue.text: None out of order in the department, he states in evidence

indicators.note: in says the shuffled word sits inside the abbreviation

parts.note: dept is the abbreviation for department

indicators.note: the letters of none are put out of their proper order

explanation.surface: No one in the department is misbehaving, a witness testifies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'None out of order' looks like a remark about bad behaviour; here it is the anagram signal. A deponent is the legal term for a witness making a sworn statement.
explanation.definitionFit: A witness giving sworn written testimony is so called in law.

parts.note: in Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale the cockerel Chanticleer has a best-loved hen among his seven

explanation.surface: A rooster's preferred companion.
explanation.walkthrough: Chanticleer is the cock in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales; his favourite wife is the fair hen of that tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer names the hen who is the rooster's chief beloved in the Nun's Priest's Tale.

definitions.meaning: a garden plant with tall spikes of pea-like blooms
Arsène, the gentleman burglar of Maurice Leblanc's French detective stories

explanation.surface: A bloom that somehow draws the attention of crime experts.
explanation.walkthrough: Arsène of the surname is Leblanc's fictional master thief, so a criminologist would study him.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a garden plant and the surname of a famous fictional gentleman thief.

parts.note: a flutter is a small wager, a bet

explanation.surface: Placing a bet by post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flutter' is British slang for a small gamble.
explanation.definitionFit: The second letter of the Greek alphabet.

definitions.meaning: a moving band that carries goods along a factory line
a strap is a band, so a strapping type is a kind of strap; read normally it is a burly person

explanation.surface: A porter described as a big, brawny fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A strapping type' looks like a well-built man; it is a kind of strap, the loop of the moving band.
explanation.definitionFit: A factory moving band carries goods, and its loop is a form of strap.

parts.note: in cricket the runs scored are put up on a display board for spectators

explanation.surface: A signpost for a climb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs up' looks like climbing; in cricket the runs scored go up on a board at the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: The board at a cricket ground displays the tally of runs.

clue.text: Supporter of the League if a lot "of witches aren't wrong

parts.note: a coven is a gathering of witches

indicators.note: the letters of aren't are put wrongly, out of their proper order

explanation.surface: A League member, supposing a witches' gathering is not mistaken.
explanation.walkthrough: The League is the Solemn League and Covenant of 1643, a Scottish Presbyterian pact; 'aren't wrong' looks like a plain verb phrase but is an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Signatories of the Scottish Solemn League and Covenant were known by that title.

parts.note: to heckle is to provoke or goad, and a sempstress works with a sewing pin

explanation.surface: A seamstress shouting at a speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for goading someone also describes what a seamstress does with her sewing tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Goading or provoking someone is called by a word drawn from sewing.

clue.text: Rotate and rock till light appears

parts.note: to eddy is to swirl round, rotate
stone means rock

explanation.surface: Spinning and rocking until a lamp comes on.
explanation.walkthrough: The light is the lighthouse on the Eddystone Rocks off Plymouth.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous lighthouse on reefs off Plymouth carries this name.

parts.note: protesters who walk in step, calling left, right, left as they go

explanation.surface: Protesters of both political wings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left and right' looks political; it is the drill call of people walking in step.
explanation.definitionFit: Protesters who walk in procession are named after that kind of walking.

parts.note: the busiest commuting time of day, the hour when trains and roads are packed

explanation.surface: A quotation: 'one crowded hour of glorious life'.
explanation.walkthrough: The line 'One crowded hour of glorious life' is a famous quotation; here the crowded hour is the commuters' peak.
explanation.definitionFit: The peak travel period is called by this word plus hour.

parts.note: Hesperian means of the west, the land of the evening star
ho is a call to attract attention

explanation.surface: A western greeting that would make a fine book.
explanation.walkthrough: The title is Charles Kingsley's 1855 adventure novel, and the Devon village later named after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Kingsley's sea adventure book bears this title.

definitions.meaning: an old adverb meaning hardly, barely

explanation.surface: A complaint about insufficient quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means rare or insufficient, and in older use the adverb means barely.

clue.text: Of cabbages and kings — one can weary another

parts.note: to bore someone is to weary them
cole is another cabbage, and Old King Cole another king

explanation.surface: The Walrus's chatter of cabbages and kings, which wearies its listeners.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening echoes the Walrus in Lewis Carroll. One of the cabbages is the answer; 'another' is cole, both a cabbage and the nursery-rhyme Old King Cole.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a curly kale, one of the cabbage family.

clue.text: Just about the last thing Richard III would be

definitions.text: Just about the last thing Richard III would be

parts.words: Just about the last thing Richard III would be
parts.note: a clause added at the end of a document, and also a horseman, which Richard III, crying 'My kingdom for a horse!', could not be

explanation.surface: A remark about the character of Shakespeare's king.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's Richard III cries 'A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!': a horseman is what he cannot be; the word is also an addition at the end of a document.
explanation.definitionFit: A clause appended at the end of a document, and a horseman, share the word.

parts.note: Humpty Dumpty is an egg, and the covering that keeps a boiled egg warm sits on top like a hat

explanation.surface: The headwear of the nursery-rhyme figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Humpty Dumpty is an egg; a knitted cover put over a boiled egg to keep it warm is his headgear.
explanation.definitionFit: A knitted egg warmer sits on an egg like a cap.

clue.text: Duck for me in the direction of the Lizard

indicators.note: in puts the word me between the compass letters

parts.note: the Lizard is the peninsula at the south-west tip of Britain, so SW
taken as written

explanation.surface: Ducking down for someone heading towards Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lizard is Cornwall's southern point, in England's south-west.
explanation.definitionFit: A small diving duck of northern waters.

parts.note: Esau sold his birthright for a dish of pottage, and a forces dining hall has the same name

explanation.surface: A question about soup on a menu.
explanation.walkthrough: Esau sold his birthright for a 'mess of pottage'; the word is also a military dining room.
explanation.definitionFit: A military dining hall bears the same word as the Bible's dish of pottage.

clue.text: Tree which, bearing beechnuts, etc., has been an objective of 19

definitions.meaning: a waterside tree of the birch family

definitions.text: which, bearing beechnuts, etc., has been an objective of 19
definitions.meaning: add mast (beechnuts) and on (bearing) and you get Aldermaston, goal of the nuclear-disarmament marches

explanation.surface: A tree with nuts that protesters once walked towards.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 is MARCHERS. Mast is fallen beechnuts; with ON the tree's name becomes Aldermaston, the weapons site that CND marchers walked to each Easter from 1958.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a birch-family tree, and with mast and on it names the Berkshire weapons site.

clue.text: Premier's address lacks nothing to describe him

definitions.text: Premier's address lacks nothing to describe him

parts.words: Premier's address lacks nothing to describe him
parts.note: the Prime Minister lives at Number 10; take away the nought from 10 and 1 is left, the phrase for the most important person

explanation.surface: A prime minister's residence is complete enough to sum him up.
explanation.walkthrough: Number 10 Downing Street is the British Prime Minister's home. 'Lacks nothing' removes the 0 from 10, leaving 1; a top person is called this.
explanation.definitionFit: The leading person in any group is called the chief or the top one.

clue.text: Again stepped back to bed here, brother

indicators.note: back says the word for again stepped is read from end to start

parts.note: retrod means stepped again, past tense

explanation.surface: Someone who walked back to bed again, addressing a brother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns RETROD to give the word. A brother is a monk here; the word is a monastery dormitory.
explanation.definitionFit: A monastic dormitory is where the monks of a house sleep.

clue.text: Torquemada one of them ? So his name suggests

definitions.text: Torquemada one of them ? So his name suggests

parts.words: Torquemada one of them ? So his name suggests
parts.note: Torquemada, the Inquisitor and pen-name of the Observer crossword setter, starts with torque, a turning force; a puzzle setter and a torturer both wrench things

explanation.surface: Wondering about the Spanish Inquisitor's character from his name.
explanation.walkthrough: Torquemada was the Spanish Grand Inquisitor and the pen-name of the Observer's famous puzzle setter; 'torque' is a turning force, and both torturer and clue-setter wrench things round.
explanation.definitionFit: Torturers and setters of tricky puzzles both wrench things, the first bodies, the second words.
